quality_flags: The DOI in the suggested citation differs from the DOI in the publication information; the latter is reported in the doi field.
The document gives conflicting arterial-diameter thresholds for bifurcation aneurysms in a figure caption and the main text.
Some passages contain disrupted ordering and extraneous publication text.
metadata.summary: This expert-consensus document proposes standardized imaging assessments for clinical studies of intracranial aneurysms treated with flow diverters. It addresses image comparability, aneurysm anatomy and occlusion, longitudinal changes, device placement, and braid deformation. The authors note that many recommendations rely on expert opinion because relevant published evidence is lacking.

conditions_covered: aneurysms with an artery integrated into the aneurysm sac
target_population: patients with intracranial aneurysms treated with flow diverters (FDs)

recognition: Identify narrowing of the contrast-filled vessel lumen relative to the expected diameter at that site; the visible FD braid diameter need not narrow to the same degree.
The document calls stenosis greater than 25% relevant and stenosis greater than 50% significant.

Lumen loss and negative remodeling around a stenotic lumen are described as causes; reversible ISS may be associated with thrombus beneath endothelial tissue, which routine imaging cannot reliably distinguish.
toxicities.grading: greater than 25%: relevant; greater than 50%: significant

recognition: Count a thrombus as being on the device only when it lies within the inner FD lumen; clot inside the aneurysm does not meet this definition.
Base the assessment on the final angiographic series or run.

toxicities.event: Incomplete FD opening or wall apposition
recognition: Assess the entire FD length, recording the proximal and distal ends separately.
On DSA, contrast visible between the device and the parent artery wall indicates incomplete apposition.
Incomplete opening is particularly noted in curved vessel segments and often occurs proximally.

management.severity: Insufficient opening in a curved vessel segment
management.actions: Additional maneuvers or implantation of a second stent may be needed.
Re-passing the device with the delivery catheter can resolve most cases.

recognition: The stent may move proximally and can protrude into the aneurysm.
Compare follow-up images with the final image from the index procedure for movement of either or both FD ends toward the aneurysm neck of at least 5%.
Unintended shortening can have its greatest adverse consequences when landing zones are close to the aneurysm neck.
The proximal or distal FD tip converges into a cone, with more than 25% reduction in outer diameter relative to the expected continuation of the device.

Do not classify a cone-shaped braid that follows a pre-existing taper of the parent artery as fish-mouthing; describe that observation in a comment. The classification applies if deformation becomes more pronounced.
toxicities.grading: F2B2: None (<25%)†, 25%–50%, >50% of braid diameter, cannot determine

recognition: Look for a localized outward bulge in the FD mid-segment (mid 50%) that exceeds the proximal and/or distal braid diameter and should have a dense rim.
Identify a bottle-necked or cigar-shaped reduction in device diameter of >1/3 across >1/3 of FD length; unlike fish-mouthing, it affects a larger segment.
It may occur with negative remodeling or neointimal lining.

management.actions: The document describes angioplasty or device removal.

therapies_index.name: flow diverters (FDs)
therapies_index.mechanism: Provide a stable framework for endothelial growth along the device struts, helping exclude the aneurysm from circulation.
monitoring: Assess neck coverage and wall apposition on the final DSA run.
Obtain follow-up vascular imaging at 6 and 12 months; further angiographic follow-up at yearly intervals is recommended at the treating center's discretion.
Use DSA at 12 months as the principal comparison with the procedural result for aneurysm occlusion and braid changes.

therapies_index.name: FD deployment
therapies_index.mechanism: Places a braided endoluminal scaffold to redirect flow toward the parent artery and support vascular reconstruction.
monitoring: Evaluate wall apposition throughout the FD and separately at its proximal and distal ends on the final DSA run.
Assess aneurysm neck coverage separately from wall apposition.
Compare follow-up imaging with the final procedural images when assessing braid changes.

therapies_index.name: re-passing the device with the delivery catheter
indirect flow diversion
therapies_index.administration: The FD is intentionally positioned in a more proximal artery without covering the aneurysm neck.
monitoring: When neck coverage is absent or incomplete, record whether that placement was intended, unintended, or cannot be determined.

artifacts.title: Table 1: Grading of image comparability between different time points
artifacts.source_heading: BASIC IMAGE EVALUATION CONSIDERATIONS FOR FDS — General imaging considerations for clinical studies

rows: Similar projections/techniques, good images, free from relevant artifacts
Highest quality comparisons, choice for questions with highest precision requirements
Deviating projections/techniques but still usable for change assessment, no substantial artifacts in any of the visits
Standard quality comparisons, can be used
Image projections/techniques do not allow for change assessment, substantial artifacts from any source in any of the visits, also related to contrast application

artifacts.summary: Classifies the comparability of images acquired at different visits as Good, Sufficient, or Insufficient. The classification separates confidence in a longitudinal comparison from the imaging finding itself.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It indicates whether an apparent change can be assessed reliably; comparisons graded Insufficient are treated as ‘cannot determine’.

artifacts.title: Table 2: Major aneurysm occlusion scores

rows: Focused on flow dynamics in aneurysm sac, mainly before and directly after implantation
Occlusion + Flow + Anatomy + Clinical (outcomes-based grading scale)

artifacts.description: Empty cells retain the table’s grouped layout; a scope shown on one row is not assigned to another row.
artifacts.summary: Groups named scales by static occlusion, residual flow, and occlusion prediction, and records the scope specified for each applicable row.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It helps distinguish scales that describe aneurysm filling from those that address flow dynamics or predict occlusion when selecting an assessment for a study.

artifacts.title: Table 3: F2B2 braid deformation patterns

rows: Movement on either or both ends of the FD towards the aneurysm neck of at least 5%
Clearly visible compared with specific previous image, no semiquantitative estimate
Converging of focal FD end (cone shape) with more than 25% decrease of the outer FD diameter compared with expected continuation of FD shape
None (<25%)†, 25%–50%, >50% of braid diameter, cannot determine
Involves just the proximal and/or distal tip
Braid bump or localized outward bulging of the FD mid-segment
Deformation exceeds proximal and/ or distal braid diameter; should have dense rim
Bottle-necked or cigar-shaped deformation diameter, decrease of >1/3 involving >1/3 of FD length
Commonly noted, acutely requiring angioplasty or device removal; as opposed to fish-mouthing, involves a larger FD segment

artifacts.description: The foreshortening footnote specifies comparison of a follow-up image with the final image from the index procedure and refers to elongation or foreshortening of ±5% of total length. The fish-mouthing footnote states that <25% deformation cannot be detected reliably in typical images because DSA acquisition angles and vessel anatomy differ.
artifacts.summary: Defines the four F2B2 deformation patterns and provides their locations, grading choices, and distinguishing features.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Consistent pattern definitions support assessment of FD braid stability during the procedure and at follow-up without conflating braid shape with wall apposition or vessel-lumen findings.

artifacts.title: Selection of a reference arterial diameter for stenosis measurement
artifacts.source_heading: Evaluating longitudinal changes: neointimal lining and stenosis
artifacts.description: Step 1: Measure the widest normal, non-tortuous segment of the proximal parent artery. Step 2: If that segment is diseased, use the widest normal, non-tortuous segment of the distal parent artery. Step 3: If the distal segment is also diseased, use the most distal normal, non-tortuous segment of the feeding artery.
artifacts.summary: Provides an ordered choice of arterial segments from which to obtain the reference diameter for stenosis assessment.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Using the specified reference-selection order makes measurements of parent-artery narrowing more consistent across assessments.

conditions.name: intracranial aneurysms
conditions.description: The document addresses radiological evaluation of intracranial aneurysms treated with flow diverters, including their morphology, dimensions, occlusion, and relationship to adjacent arteries.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess aneurysm filling, parent-artery stenosis, device position, and changes after treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The preferred imaging modality for evaluation; a study at 12 months is the principal comparison with the procedural result.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The final angiographic run is used to assess device-related thrombus and wall apposition. Recurrence and changes in occlusion should be judged only when images have good comparability.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess vascular anatomy and treatment findings when the preferred modality is unavailable or cannot be evaluated.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected after DSA in the stated order of imaging preference.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: For device evaluation, flat-panel detector CTA (FP-CTA) with intra-arterial contrast is preferred to standard CTA.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess aneurysm and vessel filling and, when image quality permits, device wall apposition.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected after DSA and CTA in the stated order of imaging preference; particularly useful when coils have also been placed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Contrast-enhanced MRA can make aneurysm and vessel-lumen filling easier to assess. Neointimal lining generally cannot be evaluated reliably with MRA.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: An ideal source for dimensional assessment when available.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Maximum-intensity projections can be used; the most reliable dimensional measurements require 3D raw data.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used when suitable images and calibration information are available.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reliable measurements require calibration factors, which may be unavailable to the imaging core laboratory.

prognostic_tools.name: Raymond–Roy Scale (RR)

risk_groups.criteria: Residual filling at the aneurysm neck.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: The document presents this as an occlusion classification, not a risk-prediction tool. It does not capture every treatment objective for bifurcation aneurysms or aneurysms containing an artery.

prognostic_tools.name: modified Cekirge–Saatci (mCS) classification
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Used to characterize dynamic flow remodeling when the study includes bifurcation aneurysms or aneurysms with an artery incorporated into the sac; no risk strata are provided.

prognostic_tools.name: O'Kelly–Marotta
components: Flow dynamics in the aneurysm sac
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Listed among residual-flow scales, principally concerning the periods before and immediately after implantation; no risk strata are provided.

prognostic_tools.name: Kamran–Byrne
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Listed as a residual-flow scale without a described risk stratification.

prognostic_tools.name: SMART
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Listed as a residual-flow scale without a described risk stratification.

prognostic_tools.name: FDSS
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Presented as an outcomes-based occlusion-prediction grading scale; its categories are not specified.

prognostic_tools.name: 4F-FPS
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Listed under occlusion prediction without defined categories or outcomes.

follow_up.schedule: Vascular imaging at 6 and 12 months is recommended. Additional angiographic follow-up is recommended at yearly intervals according to the treating center's discretion.
recommended_tests: DSA at 12 months to compare occlusion and possible braid changes with the procedural result
DSA and MRA at approximately the same time when the most complete assessment of healing, including shape beyond the contrast-filled lumen, is sought
long_term_effects: Changes in the aneurysm's outer shape
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Ending imaging follow-up may be considered after complete occlusion without stenosis or braid deformation.

conditions.name: saccular aneurysms
conditions.description: These aneurysms typically arise at an arterial bifurcation and have a clearly identifiable neck.
conditions.epidemiology: Described as the most common shape of intracranial aneurysm.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine aneurysm height, width, and neck dimensions, including any daughter sacs.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Height is measured perpendicular to the parent artery's longitudinal axis where applicable; width and neck are measured parallel to that axis where applicable. Sizes are recorded in millimeters or to the nearest tenth of a millimeter.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess residual aneurysm filling and changes in occlusion after treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Procedural and follow-up assessment, particularly the comparison at 12 months.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The Raymond–Roy Scale (RR) distinguishes complete occlusion, a residual neck, and residual aneurysm filling.

prognostic_tools.name: Raymond–Roy Scale (RR)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: An occlusion classification rather than a stated prognostic risk model. A change from complete occlusion (RR class I) to a new neck remnant or residual aneurysm filling constitutes recurrence.

follow_up.schedule: Vascular imaging at 6 and 12 months, with further angiographic examinations at yearly intervals at the treating center's discretion.
recommended_tests: DSA at 12 months for comparison with the procedural result
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Discontinuation of imaging follow-up may be considered when occlusion is complete and neither stenosis nor braid deformation is present.

conditions.name: fusiform aneurysms
conditions.description: The document uses this morphological label for spindle-shaped aneurysms while cautioning that shape alone does not identify their underlying cause.
conditions.epidemiology: The cited account attributes spindle-shaped aneurysms to a dissecting origin in 73%, an atherosclerotic origin in 18%, and a collagen disease origin in 9% of cases.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: For this morphology, height and neck are both defined using the widest diameter of the contrasted aneurysm lumen.

follow_up.schedule: The document's general schedule is vascular imaging at 6 and 12 months, followed by angiographic imaging at yearly intervals when the treating center considers it appropriate.
recommended_tests: DSA at 12 months for comparison with the procedural result

conditions.name: dissecting aneurysms
conditions.description: This label applies to false aneurysms with an irregular contour, often accompanied by stenosis, evidence of intimal injury, or underlying vasculopathy.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: For this morphology, height and neck are both defined using the widest diameter of the contrasted aneurysm lumen.

follow_up.schedule: The document's general schedule is vascular imaging at 6 and 12 months, followed by angiographic imaging at yearly intervals when the treating center considers it appropriate.
recommended_tests: DSA at 12 months for comparison with the procedural result

conditions.name: sidewall aneurysm
conditions.description: An aneurysm arising in relation to a parent artery rather than meeting the document's bifurcation criteria. The morphology assessment takes account of nearby arteries and their relative diameters.

subtypes.name: Sidewall aneurysm (anatomic)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Arises from one parent artery; the document also describes a gap between the aneurysm and a neighboring artery as a sidewall configuration.

subtypes.name: Sidewall aneurysm (hemodynamic)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A second artery contacts the aneurysm neck but has a diameter of less than 30% of the other artery; the text also uses this threshold for an artery arising at the aneurysm base.

diagnostic_workup.test: vascular imaging of the aneurysm neck and neighboring branches
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Classify the aneurysm's relationship to the parent artery and adjacent branches.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Morphological classification before reporting flow-diverter outcomes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Assess whether a neighboring artery is separated from the aneurysm and, when an artery contacts or arises at its base, compare arterial diameters.

follow_up.schedule: The document's general schedule is vascular imaging at 6 and 12 months, with subsequent angiographic imaging at yearly intervals at the treating center's discretion.
recommended_tests: DSA at 12 months for comparison with the procedural result

conditions.name: bifurcation aneurysm
conditions.description: An aneurysm arising at an arterial bifurcation. The text defines the smaller artery as having a diameter of at least 20% of the larger artery, whereas the accompanying figure uses at least 30%; these thresholds differ within the document.

diagnostic_workup.test: vascular imaging of the aneurysm neck and arterial branches
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish bifurcation morphology and the relationship of branches to the aneurysm.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Anatomical classification and evaluation of treatment outcomes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Compare branch diameters and assess whether a branch arises from the aneurysm wall rather than the artery wall. The document gives differing diameter thresholds in its text and figure.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess aneurysm occlusion and flow remodeling after treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Procedural and follow-up evaluation, including the principal comparison at 12 months.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: When these aneurysms are included in a study, the modified Cekirge–Saatci (mCS) classification is recommended to describe dynamic flow remodeling.

prognostic_tools.name: modified Cekirge–Saatci (mCS) classification
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Used to describe dynamic flow remodeling; the document does not provide its categories or outcome estimates.

prognostic_tools.name: Raymond–Roy Scale (RR)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Although part of standard flow-diverter study reading, this scale does not account fully for the treatment circumstances and goals of bifurcation aneurysms.

follow_up.schedule: Vascular imaging at 6 and 12 months is recommended; later angiographic examinations are recommended at yearly intervals at the treating center's discretion.
recommended_tests: DSA at 12 months for comparison with the procedural result
long_term_effects: Changes in occlusion and flow remodeling

conditions.name: blister
conditions.description: The document reserves this morphological term for particular carotid lesions with a half-dome appearance.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish this carotid lesion shape from other aneurysm morphologies.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The distinguishing appearance is a half-dome shape.

recommendations.statement: Use the same imaging definitions for assessments at study sites and in the imaging core laboratory.
recommendations.context: Study-site evaluations may occur before central reassessment.
recommendations.rationale: Consistent definitions can reduce avoidable discrepancies.

recommendations.statement: Provide the central imaging core laboratory with clear instructions for checking image quality and adjudicating incomplete or otherwise problematic image series.
recommendations.context: Multicenter clinical studies may contain images acquired with differing techniques and quality.
recommendations.rationale: Defined procedures can reduce random variation and systematic error.
recommendations.source_heading: BASIC IMAGE EVALUATION CONSIDERATIONS FOR FDS General imaging considerations for clinical studies Image data quality

recommendations.statement: Use image readers who understand FD procedures and the standardized definitions; provide training specific to the study protocol and imaging core laboratory charter, and retain the training materials.
Have two independent readers assess at least the primary study endpoint. Resolve differences by reader consensus, involving an additional adjudicator only when consensus cannot be reached.
recommendations.context: Imaging core laboratory assessment of angiographic study endpoints.
recommendations.rationale: Independent assessment supports precise and reproducible image evaluation.

recommendations.statement: Record imaging variables as simple, separate observations with minimal assumptions, and perform interpretation as a distinct step.
recommendations.context: For example, proximal neointimal lining and proximal fish-mouthing should each be recorded rather than combined into an interpretive finding.
recommendations.rationale: Separating observations from interpretation can reduce heterogeneity and improve precision.

recommendations.statement: Use image reading to describe findings consistently for the study rather than necessarily to judge an individual clinical decision.
recommendations.rationale: Individual treatment decisions can involve considerations beyond the standardized image assessment.

recommendations.statement: Use reading software that tracks results after their initial release, subsequent reader corrections, and the consensus process. Retain annotated screenshots with the ratings, and maintain a detailed imaging core laboratory charter and training documents.
recommendations.rationale: These records document how individual assessments and adjudications were reached.

recommendations.statement: When several imaging modalities are available from the same date, designate one as the leading modality and use the others to inform its interpretation.

Prioritize DSA, followed by CT angiography (CTA) and then MRA. For CTA, prefer flat-panel detector CTA (FP-CTA) with intra-arterial contrast over standard CTA; in patients also treated with coils, MRA is preferable to standard CTA.
recommendations.context: If the preferred modality is unavailable or cannot be assessed, use the next modality in the priority order.
recommendations.rationale: FP-CTA provides greater spatial resolution and better depiction of small stents.

recommendations.statement: Compare follow-up images with either the immediate post-procedural examination or the preceding scheduled visit, according to the study objective, rather than with an unscheduled visit.
recommendations.context: Longitudinal imaging assessment.

recommendations.statement: Grade the quality of a longitudinal image comparison separately from its clinical result using the three-tier comparability system, and explain the grades with specific examples during reader training.
recommendations.context: The document's comparability categories are Good, Sufficient, and Insufficient.
recommendations.rationale: Differences in modality, protocol, projection, artifacts, movement, or contrast administration can impair comparison.

recommendations.statement: Perform follow-up vascular imaging at 6 and 12 months, with further angiographic examinations at yearly intervals when the treating center considers them appropriate.
recommendations.context: After FD treatment.

recommendations.statement: Use DSA at 12 months as the principal examination for comparing aneurysm occlusion and possible braid changes with the procedural result.
recommendations.context: Imaging follow-up after FD treatment.

recommendations.statement: Consider ending imaging follow-up when findings show complete occlusion without stenosis or braid deformation.
recommendations.context: After FD treatment.

recommendations.statement: For the most complete assessment of aneurysm healing, obtain DSA and MRA at approximately the same time.
recommendations.context: The combined assessment includes aneurysm shape beyond the contrast-filled vascular lumen.

recommendations.statement: Prefer the term 'neointimal lining' to 'intimal hyperplasia', and record the resulting stenosis separately.
recommendations.context: Evaluation of tissue growth after FD deployment.
recommendations.rationale: The term 'intimal hyperplasia' implies an undesirable excess of intimal growth.
recommendations.source_heading: Evaluating longitudinal changes: neointimal lining and stenosis

recommendations.statement: Assess neointimal lining separately at the proximal, middle, and distal portions of each FD on unsubtracted angiograms, recording yes, no, or indeterminate.
recommendations.context: DSA, FP-CTA, and CTA can be used for this assessment.
recommendations.source_heading: Evaluating longitudinal changes: neointimal lining and stenosis

recommendations.statement: Avoid assessing neointimal lining on MRA in most cases.
recommendations.rationale: The document states that this assessment is generally not possible with MRA.
recommendations.source_heading: Evaluating longitudinal changes: neointimal lining and stenosis

recommendations.statement: At pre-procedure, post-procedure, and follow-up visits, determine parent artery percent diameter stenosis by comparing the narrowest relevant arterial segment with an adjacent normal segment, generally within 5mm proximal to, within, or within 5mm distal to the FD.
recommendations.context: Select the reference segment according to the criteria used in the Warfarin-Aspirin Symptomatic Intracranial Disease (WASID) study: first the widest normal, non-tortuous proximal parent artery segment; if diseased, the corresponding distal parent artery segment; and, if that is also diseased, the most distal normal, non-tortuous segment of the feeding artery.
recommendations.source_heading: Evaluating longitudinal changes: neointimal lining and stenosis

recommendations.statement: Consider a qualitative MRA assessment of significant stenosis, recorded as yes, no, or indeterminate.
recommendations.context: The document defines stenosis greater than 25% as 'relevant' and greater than 50% as 'significant'.
recommendations.rationale: Quantifying stenosis on MRA is not feasible in every case.
recommendations.source_heading: Evaluating longitudinal changes: neointimal lining and stenosis

recommendations.statement: Count only thrombus within the inner FD lumen as thrombus on the device, and base its reporting on the final angiographic series or run.
recommendations.context: A clot inside the aneurysm does not meet this device-thrombus definition.
recommendations.rationale: Intra-aneurysmal clot is an intended effect of treatment.
recommendations.source_heading: Evaluating longitudinal changes: neointimal lining and stenosis

recommendations.statement: Classify aneurysm location using the Aneurysm Reporting Terminology and, for ICA aneurysms, the Bouthillier classification.
recommendations.context: Name the aneurysm by the vessel from which its neck arises or the nearest branch vessel.
recommendations.source_heading: EVALUATING ANEURYSMS AND THEIR OCCLUSION Aneurysm location

recommendations.statement: When an aneurysm affects several arterial segments, classify its location by the most proximal affected segment.
recommendations.source_heading: EVALUATING ANEURYSMS AND THEIR OCCLUSION Aneurysm location

recommendations.statement: Assign a side to an anterior communicating or basilar aneurysm only when its neck lies predominantly on that side (clearly >2/3); otherwise, classify it as midline.
recommendations.source_heading: EVALUATING ANEURYSMS AND THEIR OCCLUSION Aneurysm location

recommendations.statement: Describe aneurysm morphology using the proposed relationship between the aneurysm, its parent arteries, and nearby branches.
recommendations.context: The text describes a sidewall aneurysm when there is a gap from a neighboring artery or an artery at the aneurysm base has a diameter of less than 30% of the parent artery. It describes a bifurcation aneurysm when the smaller artery measures at least 20% of the larger artery; figure 3 instead gives at least 30% for the latter category. The document does not reconcile these thresholds.
recommendations.rationale: Anatomical labels alone may group aneurysms with different flow conditions and probabilities of occlusion.

recommendations.statement: Describe a branch as arising from the aneurysm only when its contour in at least one projection suggests aneurysm wall rather than arterial wall.
recommendations.context: Part of the proposed morphology classification.

recommendations.statement: Use 'fusiform' for spindle-shaped aneurysms, 'dissecting aneurysm' for irregularly shaped false aneurysms, and reserve 'blister' for the specified half-dome-shaped carotid lesions.
recommendations.context: Dissecting aneurysms frequently have associated stenosis, evidence of intimal injury, or underlying vasculopathy.
recommendations.rationale: These terms support a pragmatic classification of aneurysm shape.

recommendations.statement: Use manual measurements by experienced readers as the reference approach for aneurysm measurements in clinical studies.
recommendations.context: Automated or semi-automated measurements often require correction or manual adjustment.

recommendations.statement: Measure sizes in millimeters (or to the nearest tenth of a millimeter), ideally using two sources, such as MRA or CTA together with DSA; include any daughter sacs in aneurysm measurements.
recommendations.context: For DSA, the document identifies 3D-DSA with maximum intensity projections as ideal.

recommendations.statement: Include the Raymond–Roy Scale (RR) in standard readings for FD studies.
recommendations.context: This scale records complete occlusion, residual neck, or residual aneurysm for treated saccular aneurysms.
recommendations.rationale: It is widely used, although it does not capture every treatment goal or anatomical circumstance relevant to FD therapy.

recommendations.statement: Use the modified Cekirge–Saatci (mCS) classification when a study includes bifurcation aneurysms or aneurysms with an artery incorporated into the aneurysm sac.
recommendations.context: Assessment of the dynamic flow-remodeling process.
recommendations.rationale: The Raymond–Roy Scale (RR) does not fully represent these anatomical circumstances and treatment goals.

recommendations.statement: Assess aneurysm recurrence and changes in occlusion only when the images have Good comparability.
recommendations.context: Longitudinal assessment using the document's image-comparability categories.

recommendations.statement: Additionally record changes in the aneurysm's contrast-filled lumen as increased, decreased, different shape with similar volume, no change, or indeterminate.
recommendations.context: Such a change may occur without a change in Raymond–Roy Scale (RR) class.

recommendations.statement: Prefer FP-CTA with reconstructions and source images for braid-deformation assessment. If it is unavailable, examine unsubtracted DSA images without contrast for braid deformation and with contrast for intimal lining.
Carefully assess FD wall apposition on the final DSA run, evaluating its entire length and documenting the proximal and distal ends separately.
recommendations.context: In DSA, assess whether contrast is visible between the FD and the parent artery wall. MRA may be used at follow-up when its quality is sufficient.
recommendations.rationale: Wall apposition is important to the intended flow diversion and vascular reconstruction.

recommendations.statement: Do not classify a cone-shaped FD braid as fish-mouthing when it remains apposed to a parent artery whose diameter already tapered before deployment; describe that finding briefly in a comment.
recommendations.context: Fish-mouthing still applies if the deformation is, or becomes, more pronounced.

recommendations.statement: Assess longitudinal aneurysm-neck coverage separately from radial wall apposition. Classify coverage as full only if the entire ostium is covered and the FD contacts the parent artery wall, even if that contact extends only 1mm beyond the neck proximally or distally.
When aneurysm-neck coverage is absent or incomplete, additionally record whether this was intended, not intended, or cannot be determined.
recommendations.context: Intentional indirect flow diversion should be distinguished from unsuccessful placement, including shortening or migration.
recommendations.rationale: Absent or incomplete direct neck coverage does not necessarily indicate poor placement.

recommendations.statement: Document possible causes or accompanying findings of braid deformation separately, including intimal lining, parent artery stenosis, and in-stent thrombosis.
recommendations.context: Deformation patterns may coexist, and their causes may not be reliably identifiable without advanced imaging.
recommendations.rationale: Separate observations can be combined during subsequent analysis without presuming a cause.

recommendations.statement: Classify FD braid changes as foreshortening, fish-mouthing, braid bump deformation, or braid collapse (F2B2) in both immediate post-deployment and follow-up images. Apply these categories to the braid itself, independently of wall apposition and vessel-lumen findings.
recommendations.rationale: Distinct categories provide a consistent description of braid shape and stability.

recommendations.statement: Also consider an 'Other braid changes' category, recorded as yes, no, or indeterminate, for patterns outside F2B2.

Prefer single unsubtracted fluoroscopic spot images for analyzing braid-change patterns. If these are unavailable, high-quality CTA or MRA may be used to exclude some patterns; classify the quality of the image comparison separately.
recommendations.context: The alternative-modality assessment depends on expert judgment.

document_sections.heading: ABSTRACT
document_sections.content: Background: Studies and meta-analyses have reported technical and clinical outcomes in large groups of patients whose aneurysms were treated with flow diverters (FDs). Differences in assessment methods make studies difficult to compare, obscure device behavior, and complicate evaluation of advances in FD therapy. Methods: A multidisciplinary group of neurointerventionalists, imaging specialists, and neuroradiologists developed consensus recommendations to standardize image assessment in FD studies. Results: The proposed approach addresses imaging in clinical studies, longitudinal assessment of neointimal lining and stenosis, aneurysm location and morphology, measurements, occlusion, wall apposition, and neck coverage. It also defines four braid deformation patterns—foreshortening, fish-mouthing, braid bump deformation, and braid collapse—collectively called F2B2. Conclusions: Broad use of consistent measurement and reporting methods could improve comparisons of treatment outcomes, communication among specialists, and research focused on FD techniques and technology.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: The concept of flow diverting stents emerged nearly two decades ago and substantially changed intracranial aneurysm treatment. The Pipeline Embolization Device (PED) was the first commercially available FD; it received a Conformité Européene (CE) mark in June 2008 and United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval in April 2011. FD technology subsequently evolved, while reviews and meta-analyses reported technical and clinical outcomes in large patient cohorts. Many newer FDs differ in construction and configuration and often emphasize easier deployment. Some interventionalists have hypothesized, on the basis of recent observations, that braid changes on follow-up images occur more often with newer-generation FDs than earlier experience suggested; supporting data remain limited. A cited meta-analysis found that publications reporting braid collapse, braid narrowing, or braid bump deformation did not define those findings. By contrast, more than a third of studies examining convergence of an FD end into a fish-mouth appearance defined that finding. Differences between studies might therefore reflect inconsistent definitions. Clinical trials assessing FD performance and braid stability require explicit variables and operational assessment criteria. Such standards could make comparisons between device generations more valid and inform device development, but remain incompletely established. A multidisciplinary panel with neuroimaging and neuroendovascular expertise convened to develop consensus specifications. Earlier publications addressed general clinical and radiological standards for endovascular repair studies of saccular intracranial cerebral aneurysms; this work concentrates on radiological aspects specific to FD therapy. It proposes an internationally endorsed approach chiefly for imaging core laboratories in clinical studies. Because study sites also assess variables during enrollment before core laboratory reassessment, both should use the same definitions to limit avoidable discrepancies. The authors expect the proposed standards to support research and undergo further scrutiny and development.

document_sections.heading: BASIC IMAGE EVALUATION CONSIDERATIONS FOR FDS
document_sections.content: The proposed standards concern how images from clinical studies are assessed, recorded, and compared. They distinguish direct observations from subsequent interpretation and recognize that image quality and acquisition methods differ across participating centers.

document_sections.heading: General imaging considerations for clinical studies
document_sections.content: Multicenter clinical studies should account for differences in acquisition, image quality, modality, and projection rather than assume that all submitted studies meet the standards of research centers using the latest technology. Restricting participation to such centers would probably slow enrollment and introduce substantial bias; this assessment reflects the authors’ collective experience across studies involving hundreds of centers worldwide.

document_sections.heading: Image data quality
document_sections.content: Study protocols commonly standardize acquisition, yet images submitted by different centers still vary considerably in technique and quality. Clear central core laboratory procedures for verifying quality and adjudicating problems, including incomplete image series, are important for reducing random variation and systematic error and for improving the precision of treatment-effect estimates. Expert readers must compare observations across views and modalities and translate them into standardized variables. The quality of a longitudinal comparison should be assessed independently of the finding being compared. Table 1 presents three comparability grades—Good, Sufficient, and Insufficient—and explains when a comparison is suitable, usable despite differences, or unsuitable for determining change. Movement and inadequate contrast delivery affect these grades through their effect on comparability. Reader training should illustrate the grades with specific examples.

document_sections.heading: Image readers
document_sections.content: Readers should understand FD procedures thoroughly, preferably through direct procedural experience. They should know the standardized definitions, receive training specific to the study protocol and core laboratory charter, and have retained training materials available for reference. Despite progress in artificial intelligence (AI) assessment of angiography, the authors do not expect unsupervised use without experienced adjudicators soon. Core laboratory assessment is standard in many interventional fields because greater reading precision and interrater agreement matter; differences in variable reproducibility can substantially alter required study sample sizes. An imaging core laboratory seeks objective, consistent, standardized, and impartial assessments. The authors recommend two independent readers at least for the primary endpoint. Readers should resolve differences by consensus, involving an additional rater to break a tie only when consensus fails.

document_sections.heading: Usage of reading results
document_sections.content: Variables should capture simple, separate observations with as few assumptions as possible; interpretation should follow as a distinct step. For example, proximal intimal lining and proximal fish-mouthing should each be recorded as present when observed rather than interpreting the lining as proof that fish-mouthing is not real. The observations can subsequently be combined analytically. This separation is intended to reduce heterogeneity and increase precision. Image reading supplies standardized descriptions for a clinical study and need not judge individual clinical decisions, which may be more complex. In the authors’ experience, local investigators reject about half of the issues identified by core laboratory readers. Compared with local operator assessment, central adjudication found complete aneurysm occlusion rates that were 24% lower in PRESAT and 26% lower in the Cerecyte trials; a cited meta-analysis of thrombectomy outcomes found an up to 15% lower rate of complete reperfusion.

document_sections.heading: Reading infrastructure
document_sections.content: Software used to collect readings should preserve an audit trail of results after their first release, subsequent reader corrections, and the consensus process. Annotated screenshots should be stored with ratings to show the reasoning for individual assessments. A detailed imaging core laboratory charter and supplementary training documents should specify definitions and reading procedures.

document_sections.heading: Evaluating longitudinal changes: general considerations
document_sections.content: The authors recommend vascular imaging at 6 and 12 months, followed by angiographic assessments at yearly intervals when the treating center judges them appropriate. DSA at 12 months should be the main reference point for comparing aneurysm occlusion and possible braid changes with the procedural result. Imaging follow-up may be ended when findings are perfect: complete occlusion without stenosis or braid deformation. Assessing healing most completely, including aneurysm shape beyond the contrast-filled lumen, entails DSA and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) at approximately the same time. Contrast-enhanced MRA can make aneurysm and vessel lumen filling easier to assess; other modalities are acceptable under local standards. When multiple modalities are available on the same date, such as DSA and MRA, one should serve as the leading modality while the others inform its interpretation. The preference order is DSA, CT angiography (CTA), then MRA. Within CTA, flat-panel detector CTA (FP-CTA) with intra-arterial contrast is preferred to standard CTA because cone-beam technology has higher spatial resolution and depicts even small stents better. With additional coil treatment, MRA is preferable to standard CTA. If a preferred modality is unavailable or uninterpretable, the next modality in that order should be used. Depending on the study question, follow-up should be compared either with the immediate postprocedural result or with the preceding scheduled visit, not an unscheduled visit. Differences in modalities, protocols, quality, and projections can weaken longitudinal comparisons, so comparability and the observed result require separate ratings. Figure 1 illustrates that FD wall apposition can be evaluated with contrast-enhanced threedimensional time-of-flight MRA at 0.3 x 0.6 x 0.6 mm voxel size, provided assessment quality is documented separately.

document_sections.heading: Evaluating longitudinal changes: neointimal lining and stenosis
document_sections.content: Some intimal growth is needed for treatment success. Characterizing it may become more important as FD surfaces and healing processes change. Because ‘intimal hyperplasia’ implies excessive, undesirable growth and has been reported in more than 50% of cases after FD placement, the authors suggest using ‘neointimal lining’ instead. Resulting stenosis should be recorded independently; the findings can later be analyzed together. They suggest rating neointimal lining as yes, no, or indeterminate on unsubtracted angiograms, separately for each FD at proximal, middle, and distal positions. DSA, FP-CTA, and CTA can support this assessment. MRA cannot show neointimal lining in most cases and should generally be avoided for that purpose. Stenosis means apparent narrowing of the contrast-filled vessel lumen relative to its expected diameter at that position; it does not necessarily correspond to the diameter of the visible FD braid. Measurement compares the narrowest lumen, Dstenosis, with a nearby normal reference segment, Dnormal. At pre-procedure, post-procedure, and follow-up assessments, parent artery percent diameter stenosis should use the narrowest relevant arterial segment and an adjacent normal segment, generally within 5mm proximal to, within, or within 5mm distal to the FD. Reference selection should follow the criteria used in the Warfarin-Aspirin Symptomatic Intracranial Disease (WASID) study. The first reference choice is the widest normal, non-tortuous proximal parent-artery segment. If that segment is diseased, the second choice is the widest normal, non-tortuous distal parent-artery segment. If that too is diseased, the third choice is the most distal normal, non-tortuous feeding-artery segment. Figure 2 illustrates a proximal Dnormal of 4.1 mm and a Dstenosis of 2.4 mm, yielding 42% stenosis by ((Dnormal–Dstenosis)/Dnormal)). In-stent stenosis (ISS) may reflect lumen loss, termed ‘true ISS’, or negative remodeling around a stenotic lumen despite full mesh expansion. Reversible ISS might involve thrombus beneath endothelialization, which routine imaging cannot reliably distinguish. Based on the authors’ core laboratory experience, MRA permits stenosis measurement in approximately half of cases; feasibility depends on FD type, acquisition method, anatomy, and orientation relative to the magnetic field. They define stenosis greater than 25% as ‘relevant’ and greater than 50% as ‘significant’. To make use of available MRA images, they advise considering a qualitative significant-stenosis rating of yes, no, or indeterminate. Only thrombus inside the FD lumen counts as thrombus on the device; aneurysm-sac clot does not, because its formation is a treatment goal. Reporting should rely on the final angiographic series or run.

document_sections.heading: EVALUATING ANEURYSMS AND THEIR OCCLUSION
document_sections.content: The proposed assessments distinguish aneurysm location, its relationship to neighboring arteries, shape, dimensions, and the extent and change of occlusion.

document_sections.heading: Aneurysm location
document_sections.content: Aneurysms are named for the vessel from which the neck arises or the nearest branch vessel. Although several location-grouping systems exist, the authors recommend Aneurysm Reporting Terminology for location and the Bouthillier classification for ICA aneurysms. When an aneurysm affects multiple segments, its most proximal segment, or ‘starting point’, should determine its classification. For anterior communicating or basilar aneurysms, they recommend assigning a side only when the neck lies predominantly on that side, clearly >2/3; otherwise, the location should be midline.

document_sections.heading: Aneurysm morphology
document_sections.content: Side branches, branches arising from an aneurysm, and the aneurysm’s relationship to the parent artery influence FD treatment strategy and the probability of success. Conventional distinctions between side-branch and bifurcation aneurysms often follow established arterial anatomy, such as anterior cerebral artery (ACA)-middle cerebral artery (MCA), MCA-M2, or basilar artery-posterior cerebral artery (PCA). Such labels are useful anatomically but less useful for predicting outcomes: differences in anatomy and arterial diameter, including posterior communicating (PCom) diameter, produce different flow conditions, strategies, and pre-treatment probabilities of occlusion even among aneurysms with the same anatomical label. The authors propose a pragmatic classification based on parent arteries and branches. A sidewall aneurysm has a gap between it and a neighboring artery of any diameter when arising from one parent artery, or has an artery arising at its base whose diameter is less than 30% of the parent artery. A bifurcation aneurysm arises at an arterial bifurcation where the smaller artery has a diameter of a least 20% of the larger artery. A branch should be described as arising from the aneurysm only when its contour in any projection suggests aneurysm wall rather than arterial wall. Under this approach, some paraophthalmic aneurysms may be classified as bifurcation rather than sidewall aneurysms, complicating comparisons with older studies; including location as another variable still permits matching. Figure 3 depicts an anatomical sidewall aneurysm from one parent artery, a hemodynamic sidewall example whose neck touches a second artery with a diameter of less than 30% of the other artery, a bifurcation example with a second artery measuring at least 30% of the major artery, and an artery originating from the shape of the aneurysm sac. The figure’s at least 30% bifurcation example differs from the a least 20% criterion in the accompanying text.

document_sections.heading: Aneurysm shape
document_sections.content: Aneurysms are commonly grouped into overlapping saccular, fusiform, and dissecting shapes on the basis of hypothesized pathogenesis. Saccular or berry-shaped aneurysms are the most common intracranial type and usually arise at bifurcations with a distinct neck. For spindle-shaped aneurysms, a cited study attributed origin to dissection in 73%, atherosclerosis in 18%, and collagen disease in 9% of cases; the label ‘fusiform’ therefore conveys little about cause by itself. Nonetheless, the authors recommend using ‘fusiform’ for a spindle-shaped aneurysm as a pragmatic morphological description. ‘Dissecting aneurysm’ should describe a false, irregularly shaped aneurysm, often accompanied by stenosis or evidence of intimal injury or underlying vasculopathy. ‘Blister’ should be reserved for particular half-dome-shaped carotid lesions.

document_sections.heading: Aneurysm measurements
document_sections.content: Automated and semi-automated techniques can estimate aneurysm and parent-artery diameter and volume, but most cases still require correction or manual adjustment. For clinical studies, measurement by experienced readers remains the reference standard. Available projections constrain every assessment of maximum distance. Measurements should be in millimeters, or to the nearest tenth of a millimeter, and ideally documented from two sources, such as MRA or CTA together with DSA, preferably 3D-DSA with maximum intensity projections. Reliable core laboratory measurement from 2D-DSA requires angiographic calibration factors that are often unavailable. External calibration, such as a coin attached to the scalp, may be impractical in most studies. A guiding diameter may instead provide a reference if its size is known to the core laboratory. Daughter sacs must be included. The most reliable aneurysm or parent-artery dimensions require 3D raw data, which are seldom available to central core laboratories in clinical studies. Figure 4 defines height in saccular aneurysms as the greatest distance from the proximal aneurysm margin to the distal dome margin, perpendicular to the parent artery’s longitudinal axis where applicable; width is the greatest lateral dome distance parallel to that axis, and neck is the greatest distance between its lateral neck margins parallel to that axis. For fusiform and dissecting aneurysms, the figure defines height and neck by the widest diameter of the contrast-filled aneurysm lumen.

document_sections.heading: Evaluation of aneurysm occlusion
document_sections.content: Aneurysm treatment seeks complete exclusion from the circulation. The widely used Raymond–Roy Scale (RR) grades residual static filling after endovascular treatment of saccular aneurysms as complete occlusion, residual neck, or residual aneurysm. The authors state that RR should be included in standard FD study readings, while noting that it does not account for the different circumstances and therapeutic aims of bifurcation aneurysms or aneurysms containing an artery within the sac. Residual neck after coiling is not equivalent to residual filling after FD treatment. Occlusion scales characterize the contrast-filled aneurysm lumen and sometimes adjacent arteries. An aneurysm with absent or reduced contrast filling can nevertheless remain unstable because of continued remodeling, intrasaccular thrombus, or a changing external shape detectable with cross-sectional imaging; no validated scale for that assessment is available. If a study includes bifurcation aneurysms or aneurysms with an artery integrated into the sac, the modified Cekirge–Saatci (mCS) classification should describe their dynamic flow remodeling. The classification was expanded with additional subgroups for aneurysms treated by any endovascular method. Choice among other occlusion scores depends on study scope and is not addressed here. Table 2 summarizes major scales for static occlusion, residual flow, and occlusion prediction. Recurrence and change in occlusion should be judged only when images have Good comparability. Recurrence means a transition from complete occlusion, RR class I, to a new neck remnant or residual aneurysm filling. The authors additionally recommend recording whether the contrast-filled lumen has increased, decreased, changed shape while retaining similar volume, remained unchanged, or is indeterminate. Lumen change can occur without a change in RR class, including when contrast-filled aneurysm volume decreases.

document_sections.heading: FD DEPLOYMENT AND BRAID DEFORMATION
document_sections.content: Full aneurysm-neck coverage and wall apposition are required for the intended redirection of flow into the parent artery and creation of an endoluminal scaffold for vascular reconstruction. FDs are commonly made from cobalt chromium, with Pipeline, Pipeline Flex, Pipeline Shield, and Surpass given as examples, or from nitinol, with Silk and Derivo given as examples. Multiple woven strands usually form their mesh. Cobalt/chromium provides stiffness and radial force and responds better to angioplasty when wall apposition is incomplete, for example in curved arteries. Newer nitinol-based generations offer greater flexibility and easier navigation and deployment, but may exert less radial force; this might impair apposition or increase kinking and braid deformation. For assessing braid deformation, the preferred modality is FP-CTA, ideally with reconstructed and source images. When it is unavailable, unsubtracted DSA images should be examined without contrast for deformation itself and with contrast for intimal lining.

document_sections.heading: FD wall apposition
document_sections.content: The success of braided stent or FD deployment depends not just on material properties but also on correct diameter and length selection and on the anatomy of proximal and distal landing zones. Complete opening is more likely when the proximal landing zone lies in a straight vessel segment. Inadequate opening at a curve is frequent and may require further maneuvers or a second stent. Incomplete proximal opening is also frequent and can usually be corrected by passing the delivery catheter through the device again. Rarely, a stent can migrate proximally and even protrude into the aneurysm; a soft FD with inadequate landing zones is one possible explanation. Wall apposition should therefore be assessed carefully on the final DSA run, along the entire FD and with separate records for its proximal and distal ends. On DSA, visible contrast between the FD and parent-artery wall indicates incomplete apposition. Follow-up MRA can assess apposition if image quality is sufficient; T1-weighted hyperintensity may also represent slow flow or thrombus between the FD and the arterial wall.

document_sections.heading: FD neck coverage
document_sections.content: Longitudinal aneurysm-neck coverage requires assessment apart from radial wall apposition. ‘Full neck coverage’ requires covering the entire aneurysm ostium and contact between the FD and parent-artery wall, even if contact extends only 1mm beyond the neck proximally or distally. Figure 5 distinguishes no coverage, which can be used to create indirect flow diversion; partial coverage, where the FD reaches the aneurysm–parent artery junction on one side; and full coverage, which requires confirmation in every available projection. Deliberate placement in a more proximal artery without covering the neck is a viable means of indirect flow diversion, so absent or incomplete coverage need not indicate poor placement. The authors suggest adding an intended, not intended, or cannot determine assessment when coverage is absent or incomplete, to distinguish planned indirect diversion from failed coverage caused, for example, by shortening or migration. Combining coverage with aneurysm location and morphology can identify these cases for analysis. Keeping placement and morphology as separate variables permits more granular assessment of FD performance.

document_sections.heading: Braid changes
document_sections.content: FDs act by supplying a stable scaffold for endothelial growth along device struts, facilitating exclusion of the aneurysm from the circulation. Long-term braid shape and stability are therefore central to imaging-based performance assessment. A braid change is a difference between its radiological appearance and its appearance immediately after deployment. Such findings have attracted renewed attention despite being reported for years, and lack widely accepted standardized definitions. Based on their experience, the authors recommend four categories, F2B2: (fore)shortening, fish-mouthing, braid bump deformation, and braid collapse. Table 3 defines their appearance, location, grading, and distinguishing features. These categories should be applied both immediately after deployment and at follow-up, strictly to the braid rather than to wall apposition or vessel lumen. An additional ‘Other braid changes: yes, no, or indeterminate’ category should capture patterns outside F2B2. Separate documentation of possible associated findings, such as intimal lining, parent-artery stenosis, and in-stent thrombosis, is advised because causes cannot be assigned reliably without advanced imaging; categories can coexist and can be combined during later analysis. Braided devices may shorten during deployment to different extents according to their biomechanical properties and the ratio of stent to target-vessel diameters. Subsequent unintended foreshortening is most consequential when landing zones lie near the aneurysm neck; further expansion and shortening there may displace the FD proximally, distally, or at both ends. Foreshortening can also accompany positive remodeling. End convergence can produce a fish-mouth appearance, more often in a curved segment when a soft stent is overexpanded at the aneurysm neck. The term should not be used for a cone-shaped braid that follows a pre-existing taper in the parent artery while remaining apposed to its wall; that appearance should be noted briefly. Fish-mouthing does apply if deformation is already more pronounced or becomes so. Braid collapse can accompany negative remodeling that constrains the mesh, with matching FD and arterial-lumen diameters, or occur with neointimal lining after vascular injury or a foreign-body reaction to metal struts, when FD diameter exceeds lumen diameter. Figure 6 illustrates braid bump deformation with medial thickening in a rabbit common carotid artery FD while an elliptical configuration preserves cross-sectional area; figure 7 illustrates the F2B2 patterns. For pattern analysis, the authors recommend single unsubtracted fluoroscopic spot images as the gold standard. If these are unavailable, high-quality CTA or MRA may exclude some patterns. Assessments require individual expert judgment, and comparison quality should receive the previously described classification.

document_sections.heading: LIMITATIONS
document_sections.content: Because published evidence is lacking for many questions, numerous recommendations rely on expert opinion alone. The authors sought common terminology and clinical-study standards where FD imaging standards were absent, and anticipate scrutiny and repeated revision. Their suggestions on reading procedures and documentation draw on few FDA documents; without substantial core laboratory research, their other recommendations represent expert opinion only. They also do not fully understand the mechanisms of braid deformation or their relationship to device design and material. These uncertainties affect grading and postprocedural management and imaging.

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
document_sections.content: The authors propose standards for evaluating and reporting imaging outcomes after FD treatment of intracranial aneurysms, including aspects not previously addressed fully. Wider adoption could improve the accuracy and precision of outcome assessment, promote consistent communication among neurointerventional specialists, and help direct research and development toward specific FD technologies and techniques.
